uniequip_002_lin:
The night is giving way, and the streetlamps are going out one by one. The only light left hangs in front of a food cart on the side of the street, swaying and flickering, steam drifting up beneath it. The vendor sits by his wok, face hidden behind the steam. He sees a customer in the distance, and stands to raise himself up a little.
'You haven't been by in forever, Miss.'
'I'm finally freed up.'
'You're a busy person. I see you passing through this street every day, but you never sit yourself down here.'
'One bowl of cart noodles. Oil noodles, curry base, two finballs to top.
'Got it.'
The customer picks herself a spot close to the stovetop, and leisurely seats herself. The cart vendor turns around, stooped over like a fin stranded on land. He ladles out soup to boil the noodles, and chops up the meat, movements fluid and natural.
'You're still open so late. Looks like business is good.'
'All by grace of the Rat King... well, used to be. Now it's by yours, Miss. Back when I was apprenticing, no one would dare open at this hour.'
'Is your medicine still enough?'
'I've got ways to buy it, and I've never dared stop. I'll get sick if I'm not careful, and that'll be a hassle for you.'
'No, look after yourself. If you <i>do fall sick, that's far more hassle for you than me.'
'It's out of you and your father's hands I picked my life back up... The fact you'd sit here to eat noodles means you think enough of me.'
'My dad's goal has always been for everyone to live good lives—'
*thunk*—
Within the rhythm of the kitchen knife and chopping board lands a heavy, muffled noise, promptly breaking off the subject.
'Sorry to scare you, Miss... The new smith here does shoddy work. There used to be a smith next door, went by 'Cleavers Leong.' The knives he sharpened cut fast and shone light. Lovely to use.'
'What happened to him?'
'Died. Five years ago, he did.'
'Five years. And people still think about him. He must've been a good man.'
'Not all that good... You could count on him, but he never held back. Never changed his mind. He made one mistake, that's all it took.'
'A very serious mistake to make.'
'You and the Rat King both see right through us. You're smart. Us people below, we're dumb. Sometimes, unwise. You'll be needing to teach us a long time more, Miss.'
'You'd listen to me, still?'
'I thank you that you didn't ask how he died, Miss.'
'You still blame me.'
'I've said it already. My life comes from out of your hands. No sense in the blame game.'
'......'
'Your noodles are done, Miss.'
The vendor carefully carries the bowl over to the customer, and doesn't move away after setting it down—he stands and watches her devour the noodles clean, mouthful by mouthful. After she's done, she pulls the cash out from her bag and places it on the counter.
'No need for change.'
'The streets are tricky at night. Take your time, Miss.'
'No need to worry, I can see clearly.'
'No, you'd better be careful. Us little folk, we need you. We need someone to follow.'
'It's late. Go on home.'
'Miss...
'I don't have the guts to blame you, but I just want to ask one thing...
'If, right now, you were back then, would you still do the same thing?'
'I would.
'I'm here now so that Lungmen never goes through anything like that again.'
uniequip_003_lin:
[Lungmen Daily Interview]
Reporter: Today we are fortunate to have a special guest—the President of the Lungmen Young Entrepreneurs' Association, Miss Lin Yühsia herself! Recently, everything seems to be smooth sailing for Miss Lin. She's had one success after the other, taking over the redevelopment of several old neighborhoods and earning the praise of our residents. Special mention goes to the amusement park—my sai lou zai's always pestering me to bring him there! Ah, I feel a headache coming on already!
Lin: It was my first time handling such a massive project, so I hope you'll all forgive me for any mistakes I might have made.
Reporter: And so humble! I must say, though, you have a good eye. Before you worked your magic, these 'laan gai' and 'hak gai' were so infamous that even big shots would make detours around our less reputable alleys... Could you share with us some of your experiences on this project?
Lin: 'Less reputable'? If any part of Lungmen is less reputable, then my colleagues and I are at fault. No one hates making money, so I need only bring everyone to one table and hammer down a price we can all be happy with.
Reporter: True enough, but they've been called 'laan gai' since our parents' generation, yet you cut out those decades-old tumors in a matter of months, Miss President. I can only imagine you have some special friends at the table?
Lin: Any connections I have are the ones I've invested in. As for the people I know, isn't it only natural to become friends with your business partners?
Reporter: And here I thought you had some ace up your sleeve—or maybe it's a trade secret you can't disclose?
Lin: Haha. I didn't realize you'd be so into gossip, sir.
Reporter: Everyone knows how gang-infested these streets are. Who knows what trouble might be just around the corner...
Lin: If I had an answer to that, I'd be the Chief of the L.G.D. by now. Though you're pretty promising yourself, to have so much information and be asking such incisive questions.
Reporter: Hahaha, you flatter me. But I must confess one small regret I have—that in just one conversation you've made it that much harder for me to consider a career change!
Lin: You're too humble. To borrow a phrase from Lungmen's fengshui masters: when prosperity blooms, bad things will naturally leave. I'd also like to use this airtime to ask everyone to support my work as the President of the LYEA.
......

'Mm, this is fine. Tell them to publish it as-is.'
'Siu ze, I did a background check and the reporter has done a number of hit pieces on you under a pseudonym.
'He says you're whitewashing the Lin family, and your new projects are crowding out other businesses from developing... Should I take care of him?'
'No need. It would be impossible to silence voices like his for good.
'Let me ask you this: If I told you Lungmen has the potential to grow its businesses for both itself and everyone else, and that is what I really want...
'Would you believe me?'
'...I would.'
'*sigh* Does it matter if you do?'
'Siu ze, I—'
'They don't need to know what I want. They just have to watch what I do.'
